analysis.one_liner: Raises food stamp benefits by basing them on the cost of a realistic diet and expanding eligibility.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised SNAP food benefits for low-income households, never got a committee vote in two years despite 136 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed how food stamp (SNAP) benefits are calculated. Today benefits are based on the 'thrifty food plan,' the cheapest diet USDA says a family can survive on; this bill would base them on the higher 'low-cost food plan,' the diet needed to actually feed a family of four. It would also raise the minimum monthly benefit from about $16 to $50, give households with an elderly or disabled member a standard medical deduction, remove the cap on the deduction for high housing costs, restore food stamp eligibility for many college students, and increase nutrition block grants for Puerto Rico and American Samoa. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its nutrition subcommittee in 2019 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households receiving SNAP food benefits, who would see larger monthly allotments; elderly and disabled SNAP recipients facing medical costs; low-income households with high rent or mortgage costs; college students in poverty; and residents of Puerto Rico and American Samoa, whose nutrition block grants would rise.

how_it_helps.text: Base benefits on the low-cost food plan instead of the thrifty food plan, raising the baseline of what USDA says it costs to feed a family [S2][S3].
Raise the minimum SNAP benefit for the smallest households from a cap of $37 (set at fiscal year 2014 levels) to $50 at 2019 levels [S3].
Create a standard medical expense deduction of $140 for households with an elderly or disabled member, so they no longer have to document every out-of-pocket cost [S2][S3].
Eliminate the cap on the deduction for excess shelter costs, helping low-income households in high-rent areas keep more of their benefits [S2][S3].

Repeal the restrictions that make most college students enrolled at least half-time ineligible for SNAP, and raise the nutrition assistance block grants for Puerto Rico and American Samoa to $2.65 billion for fiscal 2020, adjusted to food-cost changes [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a larger annual SNAP outlay; the bill bases benefits on a more expensive food plan, raises block grants, and broadens deductions and eligibility, all of which increase federal nutrition spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill would significantly increase federal spending, since benefits are set by formula and would rise automatically every year with food costs and with no offsetting cuts anywhere else in the budget [S2][S3].

The bill contains no financing mechanism, new revenue, or cost offsets; every dollar of new benefits would come from the federal treasury, which is the standard good-faith objection to expanding an entitlement formula [S3].

The 'low-cost food plan' is USDA's second-cheapest benchmark, so even supporters acknowledged it is a floor-raising measure rather than a full fix of benefit adequacy; the bill also leaves the annual adjustment rounded down to the nearest dollar [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: higher food benefits reduce hunger among the poorest households, and most SNAP dollars are spent quickly at grocery stores. The cost is a permanently larger federal food-assistance outlay with no offsets. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one weighs anti-hunger spending against the deficit; the bill does not attempt to pay for itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Agriculture Committee and its nutrition subcommittee for nearly the entire two-year Congress, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Alma Adams introduced the bill on February 26, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1][S5].
On March 15, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Nutrition, Oversight, and Department Operations, which is where it stayed [S5].
The bill attracted 136 cosponsors, all Democrats, including many senior members, but no Republican signed on [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no hearing vote, no floor action, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, SNAP benefit formulas, minimum benefits, student eligibility rules, and the Puerto Rico and American Samoa block grant amounts all stayed exactly as they were, and the federal government avoided the new spending the bill would have required. The committee leadership that never scheduled action kept the existing program intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing SNAP rules and federal spending levels

for.name: Rep. Alma Adams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a long initial cosponsor list.

for.name: 136 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a markup or hearing; it died there.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.role: Minority party in the House (197 of 428 voting members)
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors; the bill's expansion of SNAP benefits had no Republican support in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 136 cosponsors were House Democrats and none of the 197 House Republicans signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: SNAP benefits are spent on food at authorized retailers, so larger benefits and a higher minimum benefit would have flowed through to grocers as sales. Their interest here ran alongside that of hungry households.
The bill raised benefit formulas with no offsets, so the cost fell entirely on the federal treasury. That is the interest the committee's inaction preserved.
